facts.fact: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.
Carbon dioxide absorbs terrestrial long-wave radiation and re-radiates it, acting as a greenhouse gas.
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most incoming ultraviolet radiation.
Almost all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere.
The stratosphere contains the ozone layer and is ideal for flying.
Meteorites burn up in the mesosphere.
The ionosphere reflects radio waves back to the Earth.
Light gases like helium and hydrogen escape to space from the exosphere.
The normal lapse rate is about 6.5°C per 1,000 m.
Of insolation at the top of the atmosphere about 35 units are reflected (the Earth's albedo).
The Earth's surface absorbs about 51 units of incoming radiation.
The Earth radiates energy back as long-wave terrestrial radiation.
A long winter night with clear skies and still air favours temperature inversion.
High clouds trap outgoing infrared and warm the surface while low clouds reflect sunlight and cool it (UPSC 2022 — both reverse claims wrong).
The equatorial low (ITCZ) is thermally induced.
The subtropical high-pressure belts near 30°N and 30°S are the Horse latitudes.
Southern Hemisphere westerlies are stronger because there is little land between 40°S and 60°S.
Southern westerlies are called the Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Screaming Sixties.
The Coriolis force deflects winds right in the NH and left in the SH; zero at the equator, maximum at the poles.
The Loo is a hot dry wind of the northern plains of India.
The Chinook blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies.
The Mistral is a cold wind of the Rhone valley, France.
The Foehn is a warm dry wind on the leeward slopes of the Alps.
The Sirocco is a hot, dry wind blowing from the Sahara towards the Mediterranean.
The Harmattan is a hot, dry, dusty north-easterly of West Africa.
The Santa Ana is a hot, dry offshore wind of southern California.
The Berg is a hot, dry wind descending to the coast of South Africa.
Tropical cyclones are called cyclones (Indian Ocean), hurricanes (Atlantic) and typhoons (western Pacific).
Extratropical cyclones have a clear frontal system, which tropical cyclones lack.
Tropical cyclones originate only over warm seas; extratropical ones over land or sea.
Tropical cyclones need a sea-surface temperature above 27°C.
Large variation in vertical wind speed (strong shear) is unfavourable for tropical cyclones.
The IMD is the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre that names north Indian Ocean cyclones.
The Bay of Bengal generates far more cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
Cyclone Hudhud (October 2014) made landfall near Visakhapatnam.
Hudhud was an Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm whose remnants caused a snowstorm disaster in Nepal.
Cyclone Titli (2018) struck northern Andhra Pradesh (Srikakulam belt).
Cyclone Michaung (December 2023) made landfall near Bapatla after flooding Chennai.
Cyclone Montha (October 2025) made landfall near Narasapuram as a Severe Cyclonic Storm.
The name 'Montha' was contributed by Thailand.
The peak season for cyclones striking the AP coast is October–November.
AP-coast cyclones in order: Hudhud (2014) → Titli (2018) → Michaung (2023) → Montha (2025).
Orographic rainfall falls on the windward side of a mountain, leaving a dry rain shadow to leeward.
Convectional rainfall, typical of the equatorial belt, occurs in the afternoon from surface heating.
Dew forms when the dew point is above freezing; white frost when at or below freezing.
Fog mixed with smoke is called smog.
Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour to the air's capacity at that temperature.
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated.
Cirrus are high, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds.
Nimbostratus is a low, thick grey layer giving continuous steady rain.
Cumulonimbus is the towering thunderstorm cloud giving heavy rain, hail and lightning.
Cumulus are heaped fair-weather clouds with a flat base.
Köppen Af is the tropical wet (rainforest) climate with rain all year.
Köppen Am is the tropical monsoon climate.
Köppen BWh is the hot subtropical desert climate.
Köppen Cs is the Mediterranean climate — dry summer, wet winter.
Köppen (1918) linked climate to vegetation, with groups A, B, C, D, E and highland H.
The northward shift of the ITCZ over the Indo-Gangetic plain draws in the south-west monsoon.
The south-west monsoon sets in over Kerala around 1 June.
The retreating (north-east) monsoon brings most rain to coastal AP and Tamil Nadu (Oct–Dec).
'Burst' is the sudden onset of the monsoon; 'break' is a dry spell within it.
Seasonal reversal of winds is the typical characteristic of the monsoon climate (UPSC 2014).
El Niño (warming of the central-eastern Pacific) is generally associated with a weak Indian monsoon.
La Niña is generally associated with a good or above-normal monsoon.
A positive Indian Ocean Dipole tends to favour Indian monsoon rainfall.
The IOD is defined within the Indian Ocean (not the eastern Pacific) and can influence El Niño's impact on the monsoon (UPSC 2017).
Jet streams are fast, narrow bands of geostrophic westerly winds in the upper troposphere.
The subtropical westerly jet steers the winter western disturbances.
A continental polar (cP) air mass is cold and dry; maritime tropical (mT) is warm and humid.
Continental tropical (cT) air masses come from the Sahara and other deserts — hot and dry.
Maritime polar (mP) air masses form over cold high-latitude oceans.
At a cold front dense cold air undercuts warm air steeply, giving cumulonimbus and brief heavy rain.
A warm front has a gentle slope with a cirrus-to-nimbostratus cloud sequence and prolonged steady rain.
An occluded front forms when a cold front overtakes the warm front — the dissipating stage of a temperate cyclone.
A stationary front occurs when neither air mass can displace the other.
The NDMA was constituted under the Disaster Management Act 2005.
The NDRF is the specialised disaster-response force.
The APSDMA is chaired by the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh.
The Sendai Framework (2015–2030) succeeded the Hyogo Framework with four priorities and seven targets.
Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases.
The source gives the atmosphere's height as about 16,000–29,000 km.
Argon (0.93%) is the third most abundant gas in dry air.
Carbon dioxide forms about 0.03% (today about 0.04%) of the air.
Neon (0.0018%), helium (0.0005%), ozone (0.00006%) and hydrogen (0.00005%) are minor gases.
Nitrogen acts as a diluent and is chemically inactive; oxygen is needed for combustion.
Water vapour is 0–5% of the air by volume and decreases from the equator poleward.
Water vapour is transparent to incoming short-wave radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave radiation.
The blue colour of the sky is due to selective scattering of sunlight.
Scattering by dust particles gives red and orange colours at sunrise and sunset.
Salt particles act as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud drops.
'Troposphere' means 'zone of mixing'; the tropopause is where mixing stops.
The troposphere is about 13 km on average — higher at the equator (16 km; NCERT ~18 km) than at the poles (6 km; NCERT ~8 km).
The troposphere is higher in summer and lower in winter.
The tropopause is about 1.5 km thick.
The stratosphere extends up to about 50 km; its top is the stratopause.
The ozone layer (ozonosphere) lies between 15 and 30 km.
Temperature rises with height in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs UV.
The mesosphere lies between 50 and 80 km; the mesopause, at about −80°C, is the coldest level.
The International Space Station orbits in the thermosphere.
The ionosphere extends from about 80 to 400 km and has D, E, F and G layers.
The exosphere is so rarefied it resembles a nebula.
Some books give the normal lapse rate as 6.4°C per km (source: 6.5°C per 1,000 m).
Insolation is the solar energy received at the Earth's surface.
Climatology is the study of atmospheric conditions over a long period.
Insolation zones are tropical, middle-latitude and polar; insolation is zero in the polar night.
The angle of incidence of the Sun's rays controls insolation more than the length of day.
The poles get little insolation despite long days because rays are oblique and ice reflects them.
Sunspot numbers follow an 11-year cycle; more sunspots mean more solar energy.
Maximum insolation is received over the subtropical deserts.
The equator gets less insolation than the tropics because of clouds.
At the same latitude continents receive more insolation than oceans.
Isohels are lines joining places with equal sunshine.
Albedo is the portion of incident radiation reflected back by a surface.
Conduction is a minor way of heating the air because air is a poor conductor.
Convective heat transfer is confined to the troposphere.
Advection is horizontal heat transfer by wind (e.g. Loo, Sirocco) and drives most day-to-day weather change in middle latitudes.
The atmosphere is heated indirectly from below by terrestrial radiation.
Counter-radiation is heat radiated from the atmosphere back to the ground.
Of the 35 reflected units, 27 are reflected from cloud tops and 2 from snow and ice.
Of the 65 absorbed units, 14 are absorbed by the atmosphere.
Of the 51 units the Earth radiates, 17 go directly to space and 34 are absorbed by the atmosphere.
Of those 34 units, 19 reach the air through latent heat of condensation (6 direct, 9 by convection).
The atmosphere radiates 48 units to space; 17 + 48 = 65 balances incoming energy.
Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature.
Annual temperature range is greater in continental interiors mainly because of land–water heating differences (UPSC 2013).
Temperature inversion is normal throughout the year over polar areas.
Air drainage — cold air sliding downslope into valleys — protects plants on slopes from frost.
Perihelion is on 3 January and aphelion on 4 July, but this changes insolation only slightly.
Mean sea-level pressure is 1,013.2 millibar.
Pressure decreases about 1 mb for every 10 m of height in the lower atmosphere.
Air pressure is measured with a mercury or aneroid barometer.
Isobars are lines joining places of equal pressure.
The equatorial low is called the doldrums (zone of calm) because only vertical currents occur.
In the NH the subtropical high survives as the Azores (Atlantic) and Hawaiian (Pacific) cells.
Horse latitudes got their name from becalmed sailors throwing horses overboard.
The continuous subpolar low of the Southern Hemisphere is the sub-Antarctic low.
Subpolar lows are not thermal; converging subtropical and polar winds rise there.
Pressure belts shift with the apparent movement of the Sun — south in the northern winter, north in summer.
The pressure gradient is strong where isobars are close together.
Friction affects winds up to 1–3 km and is least over the sea.
The Coriolis force is proportional to latitude and acts perpendicular to the pressure gradient.
Tropical cyclones do not form at the equator because the Coriolis force there is zero.
The geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars aloft, where pressure gradient and Coriolis forces balance.
Circulation around a low is cyclonic and around a high anticyclonic.
Primary circulation is planetary winds; secondary is cyclones, anticyclones and monsoons; tertiary is local winds.
In the Hadley cell air rises at the ITCZ to about 14 km and sinks near 30°.
The Ferrel cell (30°–60°) and the Polar cell complete the three-cell circulation.
Polar easterlies and westerlies converge at the polar front, producing cyclonic storms.
Trade winds are north-easterly in the NH and south-easterly in the SH, blowing 30°N–30°S towards the equator.
Westerlies blow from the south-west in the NH and north-west in the SH and bring rain to west coasts.
Westerlies lie between 30° and 60° in each hemisphere and bring winter rain to NW India (UPSC 2015).
Polar easterlies are cold, dry winds from the polar highs to the subpolar lows.
Trade winds make tropical western oceans warmer; westerlies make temperate eastern oceans warmer (UPSC 2021).
Jet streams occur in both hemispheres (UPSC 2020).
The land and sea breeze system is only about 1–2 km deep.
The sea breeze blows by day (land hotter) and the land breeze at night.
The valley breeze blows upslope by day; the mountain wind descends at night.
Cold air draining off plateaus and ice fields is a katabatic wind.
Leeward winds like the Foehn and Chinook warm adiabatically as they descend.
The Loo blows west to east in May–June afternoons at 45–50°C.
The Foehn melts snow for pasture and helps grapes ripen early.
Chinook means 'snow eater' and can raise temperature by 5°C in 20 minutes.
The Sirocco is called Leveche in Spain, Khamsin in Egypt and Gharbi in the Aegean.
The Sirocco's red Saharan dust can cause 'blood rain'.
The Harmattan is called 'the Doctor' because it relieves the moist heat.
Houses and orchards of the Rhone valley are shielded from the Mistral by hedges and tree rows.
The Bora is a cold, dry north-easterly of the Adriatic coast.
A blizzard is a violent snow-laden polar wind of up to 160 km/h and −70°C.
The Buran is the blizzard of Eurasia.
The Elephanta is a strong southerly/south-easterly wind of the Malabar coast.
Kali Andhi is the violent pre-monsoon dust squall of the Indo-Gangetic plain.
The Zonda is a warm wind on the eastern slope of the Andes in Argentina.
The Pampero is a very strong wind of the Argentine Pampas.
The Shamal is a summer north-westerly of Iraq and the Persian Gulf.
The Simoom is a strong dry wind of the Sahara and Arabian deserts.
The Diablo is a hot, dry offshore wind of the San Francisco Bay area.
The Etesian is a northerly wind of Greece and Turkey.
Cape Doctor (South Africa) and Fremantle Doctor (Perth) are cooling winds.
The Southerly Buster is a sudden wind change at Sydney.
The Karaburan is a katabatic "black storm" of Central Asia.
Nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi) are pre-monsoon thunderstorms of Bengal.
Air-mass source regions: warm tropical oceans, subtropical hot deserts, cold high-latitude oceans, snowy high-latitude continents, and the Arctic/Antarctic ice.
Continental Arctic (cA) is the fifth air-mass type.
The formation of fronts is called frontogenesis.
Extratropical cyclones form along the polar front.
The cold front moves faster than the warm front and overtakes it.
The wedge of warm air between the warm and cold fronts is the warm sector.
Extratropical cyclones cover a larger area than tropical cyclones.
Tropical cyclones draw energy from latent heat of condensation in cumulonimbus clouds; they die after landfall.
The eye is calm with subsiding air and is warmer, not colder, than its surroundings (UPSC 2020).
Only some cyclones develop an eye (UPSC 2020).
Eye-wall winds can reach about 250 km/h.
Bay of Bengal/Arabian Sea cyclones are 600–1,200 km in diameter.
Tropical cyclones move about 300–500 km a day.
Cyclones crossing 20°N usually recurve and are more destructive.
Tropical cyclones are called willy-willies in Western Australia.
Tropical cyclones do not form in the South Atlantic and south-east Pacific because SSTs are low (UPSC 2015).
There are six RSMCs in the world, including IMD.
WMO/ESCAP naming began in 2000 with eight countries: Bangladesh, India, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
In 2018 Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Yemen joined, making 13 countries.
IMD issues advisories to 12 other nations of the region.
Storm surges flood coastal lowlands during tropical cyclones.
A thunderstorm is a well-grown cumulonimbus with thunder and lightning; hail forms above the freezing level.
Tornadoes occur mainly in middle latitudes; over the sea they are waterspouts.
Absolute humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit volume, in grams per cubic metre.
Specific humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit weight of air, in grams per kilogram.
Relative humidity is greater over oceans and lower over continents.
About 600 calories are needed to convert one gram of water to vapour.
The energy absorbed in evaporation and released on condensation is latent heat.
Evaporation increases with temperature, dryness of air and air movement.
Condensation depends on the amount of cooling and the relative humidity; air must cool below the dew point.
Dew needs a clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity and cold long nights.
Mist contains more moisture than fog and is frequent over mountains; fogs are drier.
Fogs are common where warm and cold currents meet.
Climate classification approaches are empirical, genetic and applied.
Four Köppen groups are temperature-based; group B is precipitation-based.
f = no dry season, m = monsoon, w = dry winter, s = dry summer.
W = desert, S = steppe; h = hot, k = cold in group B codes.
Aw (tropical wet and dry) is found in Sudan and Brazil.
BWk (mid-latitude desert) is exemplified by the Great Basin.
BSk (mid-latitude steppe) occurs in Central Asia.
Cwa (humid subtropical, dry winter) covers the north Indian plains and eastern China.
Cfa (humid subtropical, rain all year) is found in the eastern USA.
Cfb (marine west coast) is found in north-western Europe.
Df (humid winters) covers Canada and northern Russia; Dw (dry winters) north-eastern Asia.
ET is tundra (permafrost); EF is ice cap (Greenland, Antarctica).
Group H denotes highland climates.
Most of India is Am and Aw; Ladakh is a cold desert.
In the equatorial climate monthly means stay 24–27°C with no winter.
Equatorial rainfall has two peaks near the equinoxes.
The equatorial rainforest of the Amazon is called the Selvas.
Equatorial forests yield hardwoods such as mahogany, ebony and greenheart.
The Cameron Highlands (Malaysia) are cooler because of altitude.
The savanna climate is also called the Sudan type.
Savanna trees include acacia and baobab.
Kano (Nigeria) gets over 80 cm of savanna rain.
The tropical monsoon climate lies 5°–30° from the equator.
Over 70% of monsoon rain falls in summer.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji receive over 1,000 cm of rain.
Moist deciduous monsoon forests get over 150 cm of rain; dry deciduous less.
Hot deserts lie on the western margins of continents between 15° and 30°.
Hot deserts result from subtropical highs, offshore trade winds and cold currents.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert (about 3.5 million square miles).
The Atacama, with under 2 cm of rain, is the driest place on Earth.
Libya recorded 57°C in 1922.
Bushmen (Kalahari), Tuaregs (Sahara) and Bedouins (Arabia) are desert peoples.
Mid-latitude deserts include the Gobi, Turkestan, Patagonian and Ladakh.
Steppe regions receive 25–75 cm of rain.
Temperate grasslands: Prairies (N. America), Pampas (Argentina), Velds (S. Africa), Puszta (Hungary), Downs (Australia), Canterbury (NZ).
The Chernozem soils of Ukraine are rich steppe soils.
The Mediterranean climate lies 30°–45° on the western margins of continents.
Mediterranean climate regions include central Chile, California, the Cape Town area and south-western Australia.
Mediterranean winters are wet from onshore westerlies; summers dry under offshore trades.
Mediterranean vegetation includes cork oak, eucalyptus and the giant sequoia.
China type: south-east monsoon in summer and dry north-west monsoon from the Siberian high in winter.
Gulf type (south-eastern USA) has the Gulf Stream, about 150 cm rain, hurricanes and tornadoes.
Natal type has onshore trades all year and well-distributed rain.
Parana pine, quebracho and yerba mate grow in the warm temperate east margin of South America.
The British type has westerlies all year and mild winters owing to the North Atlantic Drift.
British-type mean temperatures range 5–15°C.
British-type vegetation is deciduous forest — oak, elm, ash, beech.
The Taiga lies 50°–70°N and is absent in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Taiga has an annual temperature range of 50–60°C.
Verkhoyansk in Siberia is among the coldest inhabited places.
Taiga forests are coniferous — pine, fir, spruce, larch — with podzol soils, the base of lumbering.
The Laurentian climate occurs only in the NH — NE North America and eastern Asia (Manchuria, Korea, N. Japan).
About two-thirds of Laurentian rain falls in summer.
In the polar climate the warmest month stays below 10°C and there is permafrost.
Tundra vegetation is mosses, lichens and sedges; there are no trees.
'Monsoon' is derived from the Arabic word 'mausim' meaning season.
The SW monsoon is driven by the Tibetan low and the high near Madagascar.
The winter subtropical jet is split by the Himalayas and Tibet; the southern branch flows along about 25°N at about 240 km/h.
The northward shift of the subtropical jet north of the Himalayas in late May–June triggers the monsoon's sudden onset.
The Tropical Easterly Jet lies between 5° and 20°N at 6–9 km, blowing east to west from June to October.
Heavy snow over Tibet leads to a weak monsoon.
The Somali (Findlater) jet speeds the monsoon towards India.
The Findlater current causes upwelling off the Horn of Africa.
The IOD poles are the Arabian Sea (west) and the eastern Indian Ocean south of Indonesia.
The IOD develops in April–May and peaks in October.
EQUINOO is the atmospheric component of the IOD.
Western disturbances originate over the Mediterranean and are carried by the westerly jet.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji exceed 1,100 cm of rain due to funnelling and orographic lift.
Jaisalmer rarely gets more than 12 cm of rain.
The Himalayas keep northern India 3–8°C warmer in winter by blocking cold Central Asian air.
Interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh (Rayalaseema) and Tamil Nadu lie in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.
Monsoon winds run parallel to the Aravallis, so Rajasthan gets little rain (except Mount Abu).
The Coromandel coast is dry in July–August and gets rain from the NE monsoon.
